director.chapterArc: A tense negotiation on a narrow embankment where Rook's declining power forces him to surrender tactical control, culminating in the group realizing they are trapped and hunted.
director.restraintNote: Maintain Toren's observational distance. Do not dramatize Rook's physical decline; let his flat delivery of 'a tenth' carry the weight. Hoyle's threat must be delivered with professional boredom, not villainous flair.

cues.delivery: Rook's admission of his physical state is a clinical fact, not a plea. Deliver 'A tenth' with absolute flatness.
cues.from: "Right," said Rook, to all of them. "Before the afternoon. Because the rule is you say it out loud before a bad piece of road and not after it, and I made the rule.
cues.through: "I did," said Rook. "And last night I sat in a cart bed for three quarters of an hour with my hands on an old woman's chest, and that's where the difference went, and it will go there again tonight and tomorrow night and every night after, because that's what it's for." He screwed the cap of the empty flask down, which he did about nine times a day now, a thing his hands did without him. "I'd like everybody to understand the shape of it rather than the number, because the number's going to keep doing that. I fill fast. I fill faster than any of you and it's not a skill and I've explained why. What I haven't got is anything put by. The flask was nine days of me in a tin and I poured it into a cup, and what that means is that from now until I stop, I am carrying exactly as much as I have made since the morning, and every night I give it to her.

cues.delivery: Rook's explanation of his limitations is a tactical briefing. Keep the rhythm steady and precise.
cues.from: "So: a tenth. Which is a man who can hold the stone, put an edge on it, and walk about. It is not a man who can put up a shape that'll stop anything, and it is not a man who can cross forty feet of road faster than you can look at it, and if any of you are carrying a picture of me doing either of those things this week, take it out and burn it now, this afternoon, while it's cheap."
cues.through: "Then you'll have burnt it already," said Rook, "and you'll thank me, and I won't hear you, because I'll be dead in a ditch with a knife in my hand looking extremely ordinary."

cues.delivery: The stranger's interaction is deceptively casual. The humor in the bread exchange should be dry and slightly awkward.
cues.from: "Everybody's north." He looked along the cart, at Senna propped up in the bed with the blanket round her, and touched two fingers to his brow at her, and Senna inclined her head half an inch. "Ma'am. You've picked a poor month for it."
cues.through: "You've not seen a man on this road," the older one said. "On his own. Buys ash. Pays over the odds for it and asks after a company."

cues.delivery: Rook's analysis of the scouts is rapid and analytical. The shift from 'ordinary' to 'hunted' must be felt in the pacing.
cues.through: "I gave him the bread and he stood there and laughed at—"

cues.delivery: Rook's deduction about the enemy numbers is a cold calculation. The pause before 'Twenty-two' should be heavy.
cues.from: "They walked south past us," said Rook, "which means the rest of them are north."
cues.through: "Ott saw forty at a table. They won't have brought forty. They've a yard hired to a date and a weighmaster counting hours and a paymaster who'll want the men he's paying for, and a section that comes out early for a private piece of work comes out with the ones who can march." Rook rubbed his eye with the heel of his hand. "Twenty. Twenty-two. Say twenty-two and be pleased if it's less."

cues.delivery: Rook's resignation about losing the choice of ground is a quiet defeat. The final line 'I don't like it' should be spoken with weary honesty.
cues.from: "And I'd like everybody to hear the next part properly," he said, "because it's the thing I have been dreading for a fortnight and it's arrived and I'd rather say it than have you all watch me not say it.
cues.through: "No," said Rook. "It's the last one on the shelf. I've had my pick of the shelf for six years and I've got very used to it, and it's off me now, and I want it said out loud in front of all of you that I don't like it, because in about a day somebody is going to ask me why we didn't do something cleverer and I'd like the answer to already be in the air."
cues.reason: Character color: Rook accepting loss of control.

cues.delivery: Hoyle's negotiation is a professional transaction. He speaks with the boredom of a man doing his job; no villainy.
cues.from: The man came up the road at full dark, alone, with his hands out from his sides, and stopped forty paces off and called out, in an ordinary voice, that he was going to come closer.
cues.through: "Four." He let his hands fall to his sides. "If he doesn't come out, then in about a day and a half we'll do it the other way, and the other way is twenty-odd men on eleven miles of raised road with a cart on it, and I have got nowhere else to be until it's finished. I'm not saying that to frighten the children. I'm saying it because you'll do the sum yourselves in an hour and I'd rather you had my numbers than your own."

cues.delivery: The final exchange is a quiet realization of entrapment. Rook's silence and the counting of fires should feel heavy.
cues.through: "Count them again in an hour," he said.
cues.reason: Character color: Group realizing their position.

pauses.reason: Speaker reset and emotional landing on Rook's admission of weakness.

pauses.after: "So: a tenth. Which is a man who can hold the stone, put an edge on it, and walk about. It is not a man who can put up a shape that'll stop anything, and it is not a man who can cross forty feet of road faster than you can look at it, and if any of you are carrying a picture of me doing either of those things this week, take it out and burn it now, this afternoon, while it's cheap."
pauses.reason: Completed thought; allowing the tactical explanation to land.
Prepares for the command to discard false hope.

pauses.after: Nobody said anything at all for about three seconds, and Toren discovered that his hands had gone cold in a way they did not go cold for husks.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing: Toren's realization of being hunted by men, not husks.
Contrast between known enemy and new threat; isolates 'husks' for comparison.

pauses.after: "Because a man who tells you he's hunting somebody isn't hunting you," said Rook. "That's the whole of it. It costs him nothing, it makes him a chancer after a bounty instead of a scout, and it means that if any of you had seen me, one of you would have said so, and the one who'd have said so is thirteen and has a face like a window." He looked at Toren. "You did well. You said nothing. You said nothing because you'd gone cold and couldn't think of anything, and I'll take it."
pauses.reason: Completed thought; pause for the weight of Rook's praise to Milo.

pauses.reason: Major emotional landing: The specific number 'Twenty-two' as a threat realization.
Completed thought; pause for the gravity of Rook's resignation.
Emphasizes the emotional weight of Rook's loss of control.

pauses.after: "Don't look at it like that," said Rook, behind him. "You're reading it as open. It isn't open. Open is a field where a man can come at you from any point on a circle. This is a corridor with water for walls, and there are exactly two ends to it, and that's the only good news there's going to be for about a day, so hold on to it."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and scene shift to the physical description of the Level.

pauses.after: "There'll be two," said Rook. "There always are."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and transition to the darkness closing in.
Prepares for Milo's realization about the enemy's preparation.
